topic: One Slow Endpoint, Whole Hospital Down
postText:
One slow endpoint took down the entire hospital integration layer last year. Not a crash. Not a hack. Just a lab-result query that went from 200ms to 40 seconds under load.

Here is the anatomy of the cascade. The API gateway shared one thread pool across all routes. Lab-result requests piled up waiting on the slow upstream. The pool filled. Pharmacy, registration, and billing calls queued behind them and timed out. Clinicians saw a blank screen. The upstream was still alive, just slow. Our gateway had no way to say 'stop calling this'.

Three fixes we shipped, in order of impact:

1. Rate limiting at the edge. Token bucket per client and per route. Reject early instead of letting requests sit in the pool. Cheap, immediate, protects everything downstream.

2. Circuit breaker per dependency. Closed, open, half-open. When error or latency thresholds trip, the breaker opens and fails fast with a fallback. After a cool-down it probes with a few requests. If the upstream recovers, traffic resumes. If not, it stays open. No thread held hostage.

3. Bulkhead isolation. Separate connection and thread pools per downstream service. A slow lab service can no longer starve pharmacy. Each dependency gets its own blast radius.

Lesson: a gateway without breakers is a shared fuse box. One short circuit takes the whole building. In healthcare IT, 'the whole building' means clinicians cannot see results, and that is a patient-safety event, not an outage ticket.

Question for the architects here: when you size your circuit breaker thresholds, do you tune on error rate, latency percentile, or both? Latency-only trips too late in my experience, but error-only misses the slow-degradation case. What has actually worked in your production?

If this saved you a future incident, hit Like, drop your breaker tuning strategy in the comments, and Share this with the team that owns your gateway. @pengikut
